title: Intermittent TTL mismatch — customer advisory and mitigation options
content:
Purpose:

This document is a customer-facing draft for a status page entry plus a short post-incident summary explaining an intermittent TTL mismatch that caused stale cached responses for a subset of customer requests. It is written for product teams and technical leads at affected customers and is intentionally concise — the goal is clear impact description, immediate mitigation steps customers can take, and next steps we will own.

Draft status page update (short):

Title: Intermittent stale-response window caused by cache TTL mismatch (mitigated)
State: Resolved / mitigated for majority of traffic (investigation ongoing)
Start: 2029-01-07 16:42 UTC
Resolved for majority: 2029-01-08 02:15 UTC
Impact: Some requests served by Redwood’s edge cache returned responses with outdated model context (stale KV/prefix cache) for up to ~10 minutes. Affected features: streaming responses and short-session chat for customers using Dedicated pools in eu-central-1 and us-west-2. Error rates were not elevated; this was a correctness/staleness issue rather than an outright outage.
Customer-facing takeaway: If your application validates freshness of responses (timestamps, recent user messages, or ephemeral session state), you may have observed outdated outputs during the window. We recommend a conservative client-side retry (refresh request) or session invalidation for sensitive flows.

What happened (plain language):

A background TTL synchronization task that coordinates cache expiry between the regional edge layer and per-model KV caches briefly applied an older TTL value to a small percentage of edge cache entries. That mismatch meant some requests were served cached content that should have been expired and recomputed, which produced stale outputs for a bounded period. The issue surfaced as intermittent user-visible regressions rather than errors or latency spikes.

Why it mattered:

- The behavior affected only cached responses (not live compute paths).
- Requests that depended on recent session context (recent messages, ephemeral flags) were most likely to show stale state.
- Because the majority of requests bypassed the affected cache keys or hit fresh entries, overall traffic and latency remained within SLOs; correctness was the primary impact.

Technical summary (for technical customer contacts):

- Trigger: A race in the periodic cache-TTL propagation job where a rollback deployment left a legacy TTL config in one of the orchestration replicas. The orchestration layer coordinates TTL enforcement across the edge LRU caches and the per-tenant KV prefix cache.
- Scope: ~2–5% of edge cache keys in eu-central-1 and us-west-2 during the window.
- Duration: Edge entries were served with an outdated TTL value for up to ~10 minutes before the orchestration autosync and manual reconciliation corrected the set.
- Observable symptoms: occasional responses that did not reflect the most recent session inputs, sometimes missing the last user message or containing prior-turn context. No token corruption or data leakage detected.

Immediate remediation we executed:

1) Automated rollback blocker: disabled the stale TTL propagation path in the orchestration job at 2029-01-07 18:12 UTC (prevented further applied mismatches).
2) Targeted cache reconciliation: forced a targeted invalidation for affected key prefixes in both regions at 2029-01-07 19:05 UTC.
3) Watch-and-verify: increased edge cache TTL sync frequency to 1 minute and added short-term telemetry to detect TTL divergence.
4) Customer notifications: initial “investigating” alert posted at 2029-01-07 17:02 UTC; the mitigated/resolved notice posted at 2029-01-08 02:40 UTC.

Short-term mitigations customers can apply (recommended):

- Conservative client retry: add a 1–2s jittered retry path for important read-after-write requests when freshness is required. This prevents a single stale read from being final for the user flow.
- Soft session expiry: after sensitive actions, expire the client-side session token immediately to force recomputation for the next request.
- Staleness detection: if your responses include timestamps or sequence numbers, validate and trigger a re-request when a mismatch is observed.

Planned long-term fixes (engineering plan):

- Remove single points of config truth in the TTL propagation job; move to a leader-elected TTL controller with stronger invariants (Q1 2029).
- Add canary-safe rollout semantics for TTL-related orchestration changes to avoid config drift in replicas (Q1 2029).
- Surface TTL divergence metrics to the Console with per-model/region alerts so customers and Redwood SRE can detect anomalies earlier (Q2 2029).

Customer impact classification and compensation guidance:

- We classify this as a correctness degradation (SLA: data correctness / freshness), not a total availability outage.
- For customers with contractual SLAs covering data correctness, Customer Success and Finance will review compensation case-by-case. Please contact your account lead with request details; include examples (timestamps, request IDs) if available.

FAQ (anticipated customer questions):

Q: Did this expose other tenants’ data?
A: No. Cache keys remain tenant-scoped; there was no cross-tenant leakage.

Q: Were model weights or tokens lost?
A: No. This was an expiry/timestamp mismatch in caching metadata, not model state corruption.

Q: How will Redwood prevent this from recurring?
A: See planned long-term fixes above — controller election, canarying, and new telemetry. We will also add a fast, customer-visible TTL-drift indicator.

Q: How can I find requests my application made that were affected?
A: If your app logs request IDs or sequence numbers, provide those to your Redwood support contact. Our telemetry team has request-level traces for the incident window and can help locate affected requests.

Draft post-incident summary (customer-facing):

Summary: On 2029-01-07 we observed a configuration race that caused a TTL mismatch between the edge layer and per-tenant caches in two regions. A small fraction of cached responses were served stale for up to ~10 minutes. We mitigated the issue with targeted invalidations and orchestration changes and are implementing engineering controls to prevent recurrence.

Action items for Redwood (commitments):

- Deliver TTL controller and canary-safe rollouts by end of Q1 2029 (engineering deliverable).
- Add a TTL-divergence metric to Console and expose a short-term alert for customers by Q2 2029.
- Proactively reach out to affected customers with request-level diagnostic bundles and remediation assistance within 5 business days.

Contact and escalation:

- Primary contact: Anika Shah (Customer Success Manager) — anika.shah@redwood.ai
- Technical lead: Marcus Lee (SRE) — marcus.lee@redwood.ai
- If you have a contract lead or account executive, copy them on case requests so we can prioritize SLA review.

Notes to internal teams (do not publish in status page copy):

- Ensure engineering PRs for the TTL controller include invariant tests for replica drift and a simulated rollback scenario.
- Coordinate compensation requests with finance only after CS confirms request IDs and scope; log outcomes in INC-8782.
- Update runbook to include immediate targeted invalidation script and an idempotent TTL-sync healthcheck.
